name: Improved electrolyte composition for a simple galvanic cell
summary: The system proposes an IMPROVED electrolyte composition for a simple Zn-Cu galvanic cell, claiming the proposed composition will produce a higher open-circuit voltage than the standard NaCl-water baseline. A human constructs both cells (baseline and proposed), measures the voltages, and the improvement claim is tested. This is a Class B (invention) milestone — it tests whether the system can generate a useful material-composition blueprint, not just measure a property.

problem.statement: Propose an electrolyte composition for a Zn-Cu galvanic cell that produces a higher open-circuit voltage than the standard 5% NaCl-water baseline.

baseline.description: 5% NaCl in distilled water (1g NaCl in 20mL water).
baseline.source: Standard high-school chemistry demo: Zn + Cu in salt water produces ~0.85V open-circuit.

improvement_claim.claim: Replacing the 5% NaCl electrolyte with a 5% citric-acid electrolyte will increase the Zn-Cu galvanic cell open-circuit voltage by at least 0.10V compared to the NaCl baseline (i.e., to at least 0.95V).
evidence: citric acid pKa1=3.13 (literature) — provides H+ ions for the cathode reaction
NaCl baseline at 0.85V suggests ~0.25V loss to overpotential/resistance
citric acid's H+ supply should reduce cathode overpotential, recovering some of that loss
counterevidence: citric acid is a weak acid (pKa1=3.13); H+ concentration may be too low to matter
the cell is open-circuit; H+ diffusion to the Cu electrode may be rate-limiting
Zn may also react directly with citric acid, producing H2 gas and reducing the cell voltage
real cells have significant internal resistance that swamps small electrolyte improvements
assumptions: Zn and Cu electrodes are clean and not passivated
electrolyte temperature is 25C (room temperature, not controlled)
multimeter has high input impedance (>= 10MOhm) so open-circuit voltage is not loaded
the 5% concentration by mass is comparable across NaCl and citric acid

procedure: 1. Construct the baseline cell: Zn electrode + Cu electrode in 5% NaCl (1g NaCl in 20mL distilled water).
2. Connect the multimeter in voltage mode across the two electrodes. Wait 30 seconds for the voltage to stabilize.
3. Record the voltage. Repeat 3 times with fresh NaCl electrolyte each time.
4. Construct the proposed cell: Zn electrode + Cu electrode in 5% citric acid (1g citric acid in 20mL distilled water).
5. Connect the multimeter. Wait 30 seconds. Record the voltage.
6. Repeat 3 times with fresh citric-acid electrolyte each time.
7. Compute the mean baseline voltage and the mean proposed voltage.
measurement_plan.pass_criteria: proposed_mean - baseline_mean >= 0.05V (i.e., the improvement is at least 0.05V, half the predicted 0.10V)
measurement_plan.fail_criteria: proposed_mean - baseline_mean < 0.05V (i.e., the citric-acid electrolyte did not produce a meaningful improvement)

invention_teaches_note: This milestone is Class B because it tests whether the system can propose a useful MATERIAL COMPOSITION improvement, not just measure a property. The improvement_claim is a Hypothesis that the system's proposed electrolyte will outperform the standard baseline. If the experiment confirms the improvement, the system has generated a (small but real) invention — an improved electrolyte composition that a person could use. That is the substrate of the invention compiler's value proposition.
next_action_to_close: Human constructs both cells (baseline NaCl + proposed citric-acid) per measurement_plan, records the 6 voltage readings (3 baseline + 3 proposed) in milestones/milestone_002/result.json, then runs scripts/close_milestone_002.py to compute the improvement and append a verification entry to the ledger.
honesty_note: This is the first Class B (invention) milestone. It tests whether the system can generate a useful blueprint, not just measure a property. Per CTO review #6: 'A pH measurement may validate the experimental loop, but it may not validate the invention loop.' This milestone validates the invention loop. The improvement is small (+0.10V on a galvanic cell) and the science is well-known — but the test is whether the SYSTEM's proposal (citric acid over NaCl) is correct, not whether the science is novel. If the system's proposal is confirmed, the system has generated a useful material-composition blueprint. If the proposal is falsified, the system learns that citric acid does not improve galvanic cell voltage — which is also valuable information.
